interest: This file provides an illuminating perspective on how major Japanese corporate conglomerates attempted to preemptively liquidate and repatriate U.S. dollar assets in late 1940 and early 1941 in anticipation of economic sanctions and asset freezes. For diplomatic and economic historians, it highlights the intricate coordination and jurisdictional friction between state regulatory bodies (the New York State Insurance Department), federal finance officials (the U.S. Treasury), and State Department foreign policy leadership. Crucially, the documents capture high-level strategic dilemmas involving Cordell Hull and Dean Acheson, showing how State Department officials recognized that a private acquisition by Aetna would inject $7–7.5 million in liquid funds into Japan, yet felt constrained from actively blocking the transaction because comprehensive freezing orders had not yet been enacted.
keywords: Standard Insurance Company of New York

overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.506, covering October 1940 to May 1941) documents the financial and legal maneuvers surrounding Japanese insurance companies operating in the United States and the State Department's oversight of Japanese asset liquidation prior to World War II. In October 1940, the New York State Insurance Department investigated the decision by Tokio Marine & Fire Insurance Company, Ltd. and Meiji Fire Insurance Company, Ltd. to discontinue their U.S. fire insurance operations, reinsure their business in their domestic affiliate, the Standard Insurance Company of New York, and seek the release and repatriation of over $2.3 million in non-trusteed assets to Japan. By May 1941, anticipating imminent U.S. freezing controls, Tokio Marine negotiated the sale of its American subsidiaries—the Standard Insurance Company of New York and the Standard Surety and Casualty Company of New York—to the Aetna Insurance Company for between $7,000,000 and $7,500,000. State Department records involving the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, the Adviser on International Economic Affairs, Assistant Secretary Dean Acheson, and Secretary of State Cordell Hull reflect the administration's dilemma over whether to discourage a transaction that would transfer substantial liquid dollar reserves to Tokyo just months before the July 1941 freezing of Japanese assets.

subfiles.summary: S. A. McCain, legal counsel representing the Aetna Insurance Company, consulted with State Department officials regarding advanced negotiations to purchase the common stock of the Standard Insurance Company of New York and the Standard Surety and Casualty Company of New York from Tokio Marine and Fire Insurance Company for $7,000,000 to $7,500,000. McCain noted that the favorable price was largely due to Japanese fears of imminent freezing of Japanese assets in the United States, and asked whether the Department objected to the sale. Maxwell Hamilton, George F. Luthringer, Dean Acheson, and Secretary of State Cordell Hull discussed the matter, acknowledging that while the U.S. generally disfavored releasing liquid dollar funds to Japan, no formal freezing order was immediately pending and negotiations were already too far advanced for the Department to make specific adverse comment.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation on Proposed Purchase of the Stock of Japanese-Owned Insurance Companies by the Aetna Insurance Company

subfiles.about: An internal State Department note regarding Treasury liaison Merle Cochran's interest in receiving copies of New York Insurance Department reports on Japanese insurance firms.
subfiles.summary: An internal note from the Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs records that a telephone call was placed to H. Merle Cochran of the Treasury Department. Cochran confirmed that the Treasury would like copies of the papers submitted by New York Insurance Superintendent Louis H. Pink concerning Japanese insurance operations. The note mentions that the Treasury wished to have this information in light of discussions regarding potential embargoes and financial controls.
subfiles.title: Note on Treasury Interest in New York Insurance Department Papers

subfiles.about: An internal routing note from Herbert Feis instructing Frederick Livesey to coordinate New York Insurance Department findings with the Far Eastern Division and the Treasury.
subfiles.summary: Herbert Feis, Adviser on International Economic Affairs, asks Assistant Adviser Frederick Livesey to consult the Division of Far Eastern Affairs regarding reports on Japanese insurance companies in New York. Feis also instructs Livesey to inquire whether Merle Cochran at the Treasury would like a copy of the memorandum. Additionally, Livesey is directed to draft an official reply to New York State Insurance Superintendent Louis H. Pink.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Herbert Feis to Frederick Livesey regarding Consultation on Insurance Memorandum

subfiles.about: A New York State Insurance Department inter-office report regarding the cessation of fire underwriting and proposed release of assets by the U.S. branches of Tokio Marine and Meiji Fire.
keywords: Standard Insurance Company of New York
subfiles.summary: Chief Examiner Charles Ryan informs Superintendent Louis H. Pink that Johnson & Higgins, acting as General Managers, gave notice of discontinuing fire insurance operations for the U.S. branches of Tokio Marine & Fire and Meiji Fire as of September 30, 1940, reinsuring the portfolio into their domestic affiliate, Standard Insurance Company of New York. Concurrently, the managers applied for the release of approximately $2,300,000 in non-trusteed free funds to remit to Tokio Marine's home office in Japan. Ryan states that no funds will be released until reinsurance contracts are officially approved, statutory trust deposits remain protected, and notes widespread speculation in financial circles regarding the future sale of the American affiliates Standard Insurance and Standard Surety & Casualty.
subfiles.title: Report on Tokio Marine & Fire Insurance Company, Ltd. and Meiji Fire Insurance Company, Ltd.
